body: Turkey uses long, white licence plates with a blue strip on the left, similar to those found in most of Europe.
The Turkish language is unique for its special characters, including Ç, Ş, Ö, Ü, Ğ, and the dotless I (ı), which is a key identifier.
Turkish bollards are simple, thin, rectangular, and plain white with a red reflector on the front. Romania has similar bollards, but they are much rarer.
Turkish road lines are inconsistent; while most roads have white lines, it's not uncommon to see fully yellow lines or a combination of yellow and white.
Many roads in Turkey have a grainy 'salt and pepper' pavement texture.
Divided highways are extremely common in Turkey, much more so than in other Mediterranean countries.
Turkish chevrons are typically red on white, sometimes with a neon yellow border, and the arrow tip usually doesn't touch the edge.
At intersections, you can often find distinctive black and yellow chevrons with multiple arrows pointing upward.
Narrow red and white chevrons can sometimes be seen, but be aware that nearly identical ones are found in South Africa.
Directional signs in Turkey use a distinct font with noticeably wide letter spacing.
Turkish snow poles typically have a black-orange-black-white color sequence from top to bottom, with small red reflectors.
Stop signs in Turkey are unique for having the word 'DUR' written on them.
Turkey uses both A-type (rounded edges) and B-type (square edges) guardrails. The presence of both types is a strong clue for Turkey, shared only with Montenegro and Israel/West Bank.
Metal poles shaped like a ladder or with a mesh pattern are extremely common in Turkey.
In Generation 3 coverage, the Google car is distinctive for never having an antenna.
Generation 4 coverage in Turkey typically features a white Google car, which may have a short antenna or no antenna at all.
A grey pickup truck can be found in some Generation 4 coverage, but be aware that similar trucks are also seen in Senegal and Kenya.
Turkey has some low-mounted 'smallcam' Generation 4 coverage, which has a large, sometimes transparent, circular blur with a small protrusion.

The Turkish landscape is diverse, ranging from arid in the southeast to Mediterranean in the southwest and lush forests in the north. A typical view is semi-arid with vast agricultural fields and limited vegetation.
Tall, somewhat square apartment blocks are a very common sight in Turkey.
As a Muslim country, mosques with tall minarets are an extremely common and useful clue for identifying Turkey.
Brick pavement with a specific interlocking shape is very common in Turkish urban areas.
Turkish area codes are geographically ordered, with the first digit increasing from 2 in the west to 4 in the east. Phone numbers starting with 5 are non-regional mobile numbers.
Turkey has O-roads (motorways) and D-roads (state roads). D-road kilometre markers show a 3-digit road number and a section number, which generally increases to the southeast.
Provincial road kilometre markers are useful for region-guessing as they display the two-digit provincial code before the road number.
Northern Turkey is significantly lusher and more forested than the rest of the country.
The northeast features uncultivated grasslands in valleys between round hills. In Generation 3 this grass is a deep green, while in Generation 4 it appears more arid.
Turkish pines are mainly found near the Mediterranean coast, but they can look similar to Aleppo pines found in other Mediterranean countries.
Tea plantations are a common sight in the province of Rize.
Olive trees are primarily found along the Mediterranean coast of Turkey.
Sunflowers are mainly cultivated in northwestern Turkey.
The majority of Turkey's vineyards are located in the region east of Izmir.
Cotton fields are primarily found in the region surrounding the city of Şanlıurfa.
Lake Van, Turkey's largest lake, is characterized by a semi-arid landscape with dry, grassy hills.
Dark volcanic rocks are a common feature of the landscape between the cities of Şanlıurfa and Diyarbakır.
Steep, barren, and rocky river valleys can be found between Erzurum and Artvin, and in the southeast near Hakkâri.
Tiled roofs are most common in the western two-thirds of the country.
Flat roofs are predominantly found in the southeast and along the south coast.
Metal roofs are most commonly seen in the eastern part of Turkey.
Sheet metal roofs shaped like low pyramids are mainly found in the far east, particularly around Lake Van.
In the Nevşehir Province, many buildings are constructed from large, light, and unevenly colored sandstone bricks.
Yellow on black chevrons are mainly found in the Balıkesir Province (west) and the Kars Province (far east).
Black on yellow chevrons are mainly found north of Izmir.
Four-lane highways divided only by double middle road lines (with no physical divider) are almost exclusively found in the eastern half of Turkey.
Vertical water tanks are common in most of Turkey but are notably rare along the south and west coasts.
A combination of horizontal water tanks placed on top of vertical ones is primarily found along the south coast up to Elâzığ.
Square water tanks with angled corners are found in the south, from roughly İskenderun to Şanlıurfa.
White spherical water tanks are found in the southeast, mainly south of Batman.
Street signs in the Ankara Province are blue with a small, round top, although newer ones can be red.
Street signs in the Izmir Province are dark blue, bulge outwards, and often feature the emblem of Izmir at the top.
Areas with a high concentration of greenhouses are likely to be along the south coast, west of Adana.
Around Bodrum, you will commonly find whitewashed buildings with flat roofs, often combined with blue details or unpainted stone walls.
Göreme is recognizable by its tall sandstone monoliths, known as fairy chimneys, with ancient dwellings carved into them.
